title: When you run multiple instances of a Spring Boot app, a @Scheduled job fires on EVERY instance. How do you ensure it runs only once, using ShedLock, leader election, or Quartz clustering?
shortTitle: How do you prevent @Scheduled from running on every instance?

s1_definition.profdef: A `@Scheduled` task is local to each JVM, so when you run N replicas of a service, each replica fires the job at the trigger time — the job runs N times, which for a banking job (interest accrual, statement generation) can double-charge or duplicate work. Three standard fixes. (1) SHEDLOCK: a lightweight library that wraps a scheduled method with `@SchedulerLock`; before running, each instance tries to acquire a named lock in a shared store (a database table, Redis, etc.); only the one that acquires it runs, the rest skip. The lock has a `lockAtMostFor` (safety timeout so a crashed holder's lock is released) and `lockAtLeastFor` (minimum hold to prevent rapid re-runs). (2) LEADER ELECTION: one instance is elected leader (via ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud, Kubernetes lease, etc.) and only the leader runs scheduled jobs. (3) QUARTZ CLUSTERING: use the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode backed by a shared database (`JDBCJobStore`); Quartz coordinates so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it persists jobs and supports misfire handling. ShedLock is the simplest for "run once" semantics; Quartz is the richest (persistence, misfire, complex schedules); leader election fits when one node should own ALL periodic work.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs four copies of its batch service for availability. At midnight all four try to generate statements, so every customer gets four statements. ShedLock is like a single shared sign-in sheet at the vault: whoever grabs the pen first does the job, the others see it is taken and walk away. Leader election is like appointing one branch as head office for all nightly tasks. Quartz clustering is like a central scheduling office with a shared diary that assigns each task to exactly one branch and remembers missed appointments.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multiple instances each fire `@Scheduled`, so guard it: ShedLock acquires a named lock in a shared store (`lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`) so only one instance runs; leader election lets only the leader run jobs; Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC store assigns each trigger to exactly one node with persistence and misfire handling.

**Professional definition:** A `@Scheduled` task is local to each JVM, so when you run N replicas of a service, each replica fires the job at the trigger time — the job runs N times, which for a banking job (interest accrual, statement generation) can double-charge or duplicate work. Three standard fixes. (1) SHEDLOCK: a lightweight library that wraps a scheduled method with `@SchedulerLock`; before running, each instance tries to acquire a named lock in a shared store (a database table, Redis, etc.); only the one that acquires it runs, the rest skip. The lock has a `lockAtMostFor` (safety timeout so a crashed holder's lock is released) and `lockAtLeastFor` (minimum hold to prevent rapid re-runs). (2) LEADER ELECTION: one instance is elected leader (via ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud, Kubernetes lease, etc.) and only the leader runs scheduled jobs. (3) QUARTZ CLUSTERING: use the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode backed by a shared database (`JDBCJobStore`); Quartz coordinates so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it persists jobs and supports misfire handling. ShedLock is the simplest for "run once" semantics; Quartz is the richest (persistence, misfire, complex schedules); leader election fits when one node should own ALL periodic work.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs four copies of its batch service for availability. At midnight all four try to generate statements, so every customer gets four statements. ShedLock is like a single shared sign-in sheet at the vault: whoever grabs the pen first does the job, the others see it is taken and walk away. Leader election is like appointing one branch as head office for all nightly tasks. Quartz clustering is like a central scheduling office with a shared diary that assigns each task to exactly one branch and remembers missed appointments.

**One line to remember:** Multiple instances each fire `@Scheduled`, so guard it: ShedLock acquires a named lock in a shared store (`lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`) so only one instance runs; leader election lets only the leader run jobs; Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC store assigns each trigger to exactly one node with persistence and misfire handling.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me explain why the problem happens and then each fix, the way I would when a team moves a scheduled job from one instance to a horizontally-scaled deployment.

The root cause: `@Scheduled` is per-JVM. Spring's scheduler lives inside each application instance and knows nothing about other instances. So with four replicas, the midnight cron fires four times — once per replica. For an idempotent read it is merely wasteful; for a job that writes (accrues interest, generates statements, sends emails) it duplicates financial effects. This is unacceptable in banking.

SHEDLOCK is the lightest fix and my default for simple "run once across the cluster" needs. I add the ShedLock dependency, point it at a shared `LockProvider` (commonly a `shedlock` table in the same database), enable it with `@EnableSchedulerLock`, and annotate the scheduled method with `@SchedulerLock`.

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 0 * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "nightlyStatements",
               lockAtMostFor = "PT30M",   // safety: auto-release after 30 min if the holder crashes
               lockAtLeastFor = "PT5M")   // hold at least 5 min to prevent a fast second run
public void generateStatements() { /* runs on exactly ONE instance */ }
```

How it works: at the trigger, every instance tries to INSERT/UPDATE a row named `nightlyStatements` in the shared lock table. The database's atomicity ensures only one wins; the winner runs the job, the losers find the lock held and skip. `lockAtMostFor` is critical — if the winning instance crashes mid-job, the lock would otherwise be held forever, so it auto-expires after that duration. `lockAtLeastFor` prevents a job that finishes in milliseconds from being re-run by another instance within the same trigger window due to clock skew. ShedLock guarantees "at most once" per trigger; it does NOT provide retry or persistence of the job itself.

LEADER ELECTION designates a single instance as the leader; only the leader executes scheduled jobs, and if it dies another instance takes over. The election backend can be ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud (Consul/ZooKeeper), or a Kubernetes lease. In the scheduled method I check `if (leaderContext.isLeader())` before doing work, or I start/stop the scheduler based on leadership. This suits the case where ONE node should own all periodic work (and perhaps other singleton responsibilities), rather than locking each job individually.

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 0 * * *")
public void generateStatements() {
    if (!leadership.isLeader()) return;   // only the elected leader runs it
    doGenerate();
}
```

QUARTZ CLUSTERING is the richest option. I use the Quartz scheduler (Spring Boot has a starter) configured in clustered mode with a `JDBCJobStore` on a shared database. All nodes share the Quartz tables; Quartz's row locking ensures each trigger fires on exactly one node. Beyond "run once", Quartz gives persistent jobs (schedules survive restarts), misfire handling (if all nodes were down at trigger time, it can run late or skip per policy), and rich scheduling (calendars, complex triggers). The cost is operational complexity and extra tables.

```properties
spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.scheduler.instanceId=AUTO
```

Choosing between them: ShedLock for simple, in-process `@Scheduled` jobs that must run once — minimal setup, just a lock table. Quartz when I need durability, misfire handling, dynamic scheduling, or clustering as a first-class feature. Leader election when a single node should own a set of singleton responsibilities, not just one job. A senior caution for all three: the job must still be IDEMPOTENT where possible, because even "run once" mechanisms can have edge cases (a lock expiring mid-run, a leadership flip), and idempotency is the ultimate safety net. I also keep the lock/leadership store HIGHLY AVAILABLE, because if it is down the job may not run at all — I monitor and alert on both duplicate runs and missed runs.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe exactly what broke when National Bank of India scaled its batch service.

Problem 1 — statements were generated four times. The statement-generation service was deployed as four replicas for availability. The midnight `@Scheduled` cron fired on all four, so every customer received four identical statements and four notification emails. This is exactly the per-JVM scheduling problem.

Problem 2 — we needed the simplest reliable fix first. The team did not want to introduce ZooKeeper or Quartz immediately; they wanted a minimal change that guaranteed single execution. This is exactly where ShedLock fits: add a lock table and an annotation, and only one instance runs the job.

Problem 3 — a crash must not wedge the lock forever. If the winning instance crashed mid-run, the lock could block all future runs. This is exactly what `lockAtMostFor` solves: the lock auto-expires so a later trigger can proceed.

Problem 4 — even with the lock, the job had to be safe to re-run. Edge cases (lock expiry, clock skew) could theoretically cause an overlap. This is exactly the idempotency safety net: statement generation upserts by customer and period, so a duplicate attempt produces no duplicate output.

The project also records that for richer needs (persistent schedules, misfire handling) the team would move to Quartz clustering, and for owning multiple singleton tasks they would use leader election — but ShedLock was the right first fix.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `StatementJob` with a `@Scheduled` method guarded by `@SchedulerLock(name = "statementGeneration", lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor)`. A ShedLock `LockProvider` is configured against a shared database `shedlock` table. The `StatementService` generates statements idempotently (upsert by customer and period). Because this chapter's tests run without a live cluster, a `SimulatedCluster` test harness models several instances racing for the lock and verifies only one wins. A test also checks the idempotent upsert. The configuration shows the lock table DDL and the ShedLock beans, with comments explaining `lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`, and notes Quartz/leader-election as alternatives.

```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is the monthly statement cron firing across a four-instance cluster that shares one database.

Step 1 — all four fire. At midnight on the first of the month, the `@Scheduled` cron triggers independently inside all four JVMs, because scheduling is per-instance. Without a guard, all four would generate statements.

Step 2 — all four race for the lock. Each instance's `@SchedulerLock` tries to acquire the lock named `statementGeneration` by writing a row in the shared `shedlock` table with a `lock_until` of now plus `lockAtMostFor` (thirty minutes). The database makes this atomic: exactly one instance's write succeeds; the other three see the lock is held and their `@Scheduled` method returns immediately without running the job.

Step 3 — the winner runs. The instance that acquired the lock logs that it holds it and calls `statementService.generateForPeriod(...)`. It upserts a statement row per customer keyed by customer and period. Because the key is (customer, period), re-running would not create duplicates — the idempotency safety net.

Step 4 — safety on crash. The lock carries `lockAtMostFor = PT30M`. If the winning instance crashed mid-run, the lock would not be held forever; after thirty minutes it auto-expires in the shared table, so a future trigger (or an operator-initiated re-run) can acquire it and proceed. This prevents a wedged job.

Step 5 — safety on skew. The lock also carries `lockAtLeastFor = PT5M`, so even if the job finishes in milliseconds the lock stays held for at least five minutes. This stops a second instance, whose clock might be slightly ahead, from acquiring the just-released lock and running the job again within the same window.

Step 6 — alternatives for richer needs. The project notes that if we later needed persistent schedules, misfire handling, or dynamic scheduling, we would move to Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC job store; and if one node should own all singleton periodic work, we would use leader election. For simple run-once semantics, ShedLock was the right, minimal choice.

```
2026-10-24 01:09:40 INFO  StatementJob - [instance-8375] acquired lock 'statementGeneration' (lock_until=+30m)
2026-10-24 01:09:40 INFO  StatementJob - [instance holds lock] Generating statements for 2026-09
2026-10-24 01:09:40 INFO  StatementService - Generated 2 statements for 2026-09 (idempotent upsert)
2026-10-24 01:09:40 FINE  StatementJob - [instance-8374/8376/8377] lock held elsewhere → skipped (no duplicate run)
```

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core problem is that a Scheduled task is local to each JVM, so when I run several replicas of a service for availability, the trigger fires inside every replica and the job runs once per instance. For a banking job that writes data, like generating statements or accruing interest, that means duplicated financial effects, which is unacceptable. There are three standard fixes. ShedLock is the lightest: I add a shared lock store, usually a small table in the same database, enable scheduler locking, and annotate the method with SchedulerLock giving it a name, a lockAtMostFor, and a lockAtLeastFor. At the trigger every instance tries to acquire the named lock atomically in the shared store; exactly one wins and runs the job, and the rest skip. Leader election makes one instance the leader so only the leader runs scheduled work, which suits a node that should own all singleton responsibilities. Quartz clustering uses the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode with a shared JDBC job store, so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it additionally gives persistent schedules, misfire handling, and rich triggers.

The two ShedLock timers matter and interviewers probe them. lockAtMostFor is a safety expiry: if the instance holding the lock crashes mid-run, the lock auto-releases after that duration so a later trigger is not blocked forever. lockAtLeastFor is a minimum hold that guards against clock skew, so a job that finishes in milliseconds cannot be picked up and re-run by a second instance within the same window.

In our statement-batch service at National Bank of India, four replicas were each generating every customer's statement, so customers received four copies. We fixed it with ShedLock as the minimal change, guarding the monthly job with a named lock whose lockAtMostFor auto-releases a crashed holder. Crucially I kept the job idempotent, upserting statements by customer and period, because even a run-once mechanism can have edge cases around lock expiry or a leadership flip, and idempotency is the ultimate safety net. I choose ShedLock for simple run-once needs, Quartz clustering when I need persistence and misfire handling, and leader election when one node should own a whole set of periodic tasks, and in every case I monitor and alert on both duplicate runs and missed runs because a dead lock store can also prevent the job from running at all.

keyPoints: ShedLock: distributed lock — only one instance runs the job
